quiz.question: What is the main purpose of threat modeling?
options: Guarantee the system has no vulnerabilities
Identify plausible threats and decide how to address them
List security products that must be installed
quiz.explanation: Threat modeling is a structured, proactive methodology to understand system architecture, identify plausible threats, and select appropriate defensive controls before deployment. It does not guarantee zero vulnerabilities nor replace security testing.

quiz.question: Which term describes a weakness that may be exploited?
quiz.explanation: A vulnerability is a weakness or flaw in system design, implementation, configuration, or operational process that can be exploited by an adversary to violate a security policy.

quiz.question: In STRIDE, what does information disclosure primarily threaten?
quiz.explanation: In the STRIDE model, Information Disclosure directly violates Confidentiality—the property that sensitive information is accessible only to authorized entities.

quiz.question: What is the main purpose of a trust boundary in a threat model?
options: To show a visual separation for decoration
To identify where different security assumptions or trust contexts meet
quiz.explanation: A trust boundary represents a perimeter or transition where components, data, or control cross between different privilege levels or security assumptions (e.g., untrusted client browser crossing into the private backend API).

quiz.question: Which statement about attack surfaces is correct?
options: Every exposed endpoint is automatically vulnerable
Attack surface includes interfaces and pathways through which a system can be accessed or affected
Only public websites have attack surfaces
An attack surface is the same as a risk score
quiz.explanation: An attack surface is the totality of reachable interfaces, endpoints, protocols, and pathways through which an adversary can interact with or influence a system. An exposed interface is not automatically a vulnerability if properly authenticated and authorized.

quiz.question: What is the difference between inherent and residual risk?
options: Inherent risk considers the risk before relevant controls; residual risk is what remains after controls are considered
Inherent risk only applies to network devices
quiz.explanation: Inherent risk is the raw risk level assessed prior to considering defensive safeguards. Residual risk is the risk that remains after existing or planned security controls are applied.

quiz.question: Which NIST CSF 2.0 function was added to emphasize organizational cybersecurity governance?
quiz.explanation: NIST CSF 2.0 introduced 'Govern' (GV) as a brand new sixth core function to explicitly establish organizational risk management strategy, policies, oversight, and executive accountability.

quiz.question: An application hides an admin button but its backend still permits an ordinary user to perform the action. Which principle is most directly violated?
quiz.explanation: Complete Mediation requires that every access request must be validated against security policies on the server side on every invocation. Hiding a button in the frontend is a cosmetic UI convenience, not a security control.

quiz.question: What does risk transfer or sharing mean?
options: The underlying risk and every legal responsibility disappear
Some financial or contractual consequences may be allocated to another party, without necessarily removing the underlying risk
The organization must ignore the risk
The system must be taken offline permanently
quiz.explanation: Risk transfer or sharing (e.g., cyber insurance or outsourcing to managed cloud providers) allocates certain financial or operational burdens to a third party. However, it does not magically eliminate the underlying vulnerability or absolve statutory legal liabilities.

quiz.question: A vulnerability scanner reports a serious issue. What should the analyst do next?
options: Validate the evidence and assess the affected asset, exposure, impact and existing controls
quiz.explanation: Scanners generate false positives and lack environmental context. A professional security analyst safely verifies the report, evaluates reachability, affected assets, business impact, and existing compensating controls before assigning risk priority.

quiz.question: Which activity primarily maps components, data stores, data flows and trust boundaries?
quiz.explanation: Data-Flow Diagramming (DFD) visually decomposes a system into external entities, processes, data stores, data flows, and trust boundaries to support structured threat modeling.

quiz.question: Which is a suitable example of residual risk?
options: A risk remaining after controls have been implemented and evaluated
A backup that has never been tested
quiz.explanation: Residual risk is the risk that persists after all existing or planned controls (such as MFA, encryption, and firewalls) have been designed, implemented, and evaluated.

theorySections.title: Module Learning Objectives & Outcomes
paragraphs: By the conclusion of this module, learners will be able to systematically construct threat models, map complex attack surfaces, prioritize risk using evidence, and justify defensive controls:

theorySections.title: Lesson 1.1: What is Security Engineering?
paragraphs: Security engineering is the discipline of designing, implementing, evaluating, and maintaining systems so that they resist unacceptable harm under realistic adversarial conditions. It is not an afterthought or a final checklist before production; it is an intrinsic systems-engineering discipline throughout the entire software and operational lifecycle (formalized in NIST SP 800-160 Volume 1 Revision 1).

Builds features rapidly without threat modeling. Deploys code to production and performs security testing only after a major vulnerability or breach is reported. Remediation is chaotic, expensive, and often breaks existing user workflows.

Identifies sensitive assets during architectural design, defines access-control requirements, analyzes trust boundaries, models threats using STRIDE, and verifies that safeguards work continuously after deployment.
The classical CIA triad defines confidentiality, integrity, and availability. Modern enterprise engineering expands this into comprehensive operational properties:
Defines required or permitted behavior. "Only authorized course mentors may publish assessment grades; grades cannot be modified once certified."
The specific technical apparatus. "A Node.js RBAC middleware verifying JWT role claims and issuing parameterized UPDATE queries."
The holistic operational safeguard intended to modify risk. "Dual-custody grade approval combined with immutable SIEM logging and quarterly access reviews."

theorySections.title: Lesson 2.1–2.10: Architectural Principles of Secure Systems
paragraphs: Derived from the landmark Saltzer and Schroeder (1975) engineering principles and modern Zero Trust guidance, these ten rules govern defensive system architecture:
Every user, background daemon, API token, and microservice must possess only the minimum privileges required to execute its duty. A background report generator must not hold DB administrative rights.
Deploy layered, overlapping safeguards so that the failure of any single control (e.g. WAF bypass) is mitigated by subsequent layers (server-side checks, DB encryption, VPC network segmentation).
Systems must ship in the most secure configuration out of the box. If an authorization check encounters an unhandled exception, it must fail closed and DENY access rather than allowing it.
Every access attempt to every resource must be checked on the server side on every invocation. Client-side button hiding is a usability convenience, not a security control.
Keep designs as simple as practical. Complex code paths, convoluted authentication state machines, and obscure protocols create hidden failure modes that are impossible to test.
High-impact administrative actions (such as publishing official certifications or changing billing gateways) require dual-custody approval to prevent single-account compromise abuse.
Decommission legacy API versions, strip unused debug endpoints, close open ports, and remove unneeded dependencies. An interface that does not exist cannot be exploited.
Document and challenge all implicit architectural assumptions. Never assume internal traffic is clean or that a third-party API will never be compromised or change behavior.
"Never trust, always verify." Network location (e.g., VPN or private subnet) confers zero implicit trust. Every single request must establish identity, authorization, and encryption.

Prevention is necessary, but breaches and outages still occur. Systems must be engineered for graceful degradation, automated failover, and verified backups. A backup that has never been restored in a rehearsal is not a backup—it is an untested hypothesis.

theorySections.title: Lesson 5.1–5.6: Five Attack Surface Domains & Change-Driven Modeling
paragraphs: An attack surface is the totality of reachable interfaces, routes, endpoints, protocols, background daemons, and third-party integrations through which an attacker could attempt to manipulate a system.
Public IPv4/IPv6 addresses, open ports (80, 443, 22), routing tables, VPN gateways, DNS records. Defense: Zero public SSH, Cloudflare edge proxy, strict security group egress rules.
HTTP REST routes, GraphQL schemas, file upload handlers, error pages, WebSocket streams. Defense: Input validation (Zod), parameterized queries, server-side object ownership checks.
Login endpoints, password reset flows, session token cookies, OAuth callback handlers, IAM roles. Defense: FIDO2 passkeys, rate limiting, HttpOnly/SameSite cookies, short-lived tokens.
AWS IAM roles, S3 bucket policies, container orchestration ports, Kubernetes API server. Defense: S3 Block Public Access, customer-managed KMS keys, non-root container users.
NPM / PyPI dependencies, GitHub Actions workflows, build runner environments, signing keys. Defense: Dependency lockfiles, automated Dependabot scans, pinned SHA actions, artifact provenance.
Every newly exposed endpoint increases cognitive load, maintenance debt, and exploit potential. Always demand a justified business purpose before exposing any interface.

theorySections.title: Lesson 6.1–6.8: Likelihood, Impact, Risk Appetite & Treatment
paragraphs: Risk management is the systematic process of identifying, evaluating, prioritizing, and responding to risks in a manner that protects business value. Technical flaws do not equal business risk until evaluated in environmental context:

The natural risk level present in an activity or system before any defensive controls, safeguards, or policies are factored in. Example: Storing unencrypted interview transcripts on an internet-facing server.
The risk that persists after all implemented controls have been applied and evaluated. Residual risk is never zero; controls can fail, be bypassed, or suffer configuration drift.

theorySections.title: LearnSphere Architecture Assessment & Threat Modeling
paragraphs: Platform Context: LearnSphere provides online courses, resume evaluations, coding sandboxes, and AI-assisted interview assessment reports. Its architecture comprises a React SPA frontend, an API Gateway reverse proxy, Express microservices, a PostgreSQL cluster, S3 document storage, and an external third-party AI feedback service.

theorySections.title: Capstone: Threat-Model and Manage Risk for LearnSphere
paragraphs: Students execute a full, end-to-end security assessment for the LearnSphere application. The deliverable represents the complete reasoning process—from understanding assets and mapping DFD trust boundaries to defining verifiable security requirements and maintaining an evidence-backed risk register.
